Content:
Cramer's Rule is a method for solving a linear system of equations using determinants.

Content:
Suppose we have a square system of linear equations
[MATH: {a_{11}x + a_{12}y = b_{1}; a_{21}x + a_{22}y = b_{2},]
where [MATH: |a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}|] Then Cramer's rule states that
[MATH: x = \dfrac{D_x}{D}, \qquad y = \dfrac{D_y}{D}]
is the unique solution of the system, where
[MATH: |b_{1}|a_{12}; b_{2}|a_{22}|]

Content:
For example, let's use Cramer's rule to solve the following system of equations:

Content:
[MATH: {3x− 2y = − 1; − 1x + 2y = 3]

Content:
We start by finding the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

Content:
[MATH: D|=|3|− 2; − 1|2|; = 3 ⋅ 2 − (− 1) ⋅ (− 2); = 4]

Content:
Now, we compute [MATH: D_x] and [MATH: D_y\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: D_{x}|=|− 1|− 2; 3|2|; = (− 1) ⋅ 2 − 3 ⋅ (− 2); = 4; D_{y}|=|3|− 1; − 1|3|; = 3 ⋅ 3 − (− 1) ⋅ (− 1); = 8]

Content:
Finally, the solution to the system is given by
[MATH: x|= (D_{x})/(D) = (4)/(4) = 1,; y|= (D_{y})/(D) = (8)/(4) = 2.]

Content:
It is common to write the solutions to a linear system as a vector. So, in this case, we have
[MATH: \left< x,y \right> = \left< 1,2 \right>.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Cramer's Rule is a method for solving a linear system of equations using determinants.

Content:
Suppose we have a square system of linear equations
[MATH: {a_{11}x + a_{12}y = b_{1}; a_{21}x + a_{22}y = b_{2},]
where [MATH: |a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}|] Then Cramer's rule states that
[MATH: x = \dfrac{D_x}{D}, \qquad y = \dfrac{D_y}{D}]
is the unique solution of the system, where
[MATH: |b_{1}|a_{12}; b_{2}|a_{22}|]

Content:
For example, let's use Cramer's rule to solve the following system of equations:

Content:
[MATH: {3x− 2y = − 1; − 1x + 2y = 3]

Content:
We start by finding the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

Content:
[MATH: D|=|3|− 2; − 1|2|; = 3 ⋅ 2 − (− 1) ⋅ (− 2); = 4]

Content:
Now, we compute [MATH: D_x] and [MATH: D_y\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: D_{x}|=|− 1|− 2; 3|2|; = (− 1) ⋅ 2 − 3 ⋅ (− 2); = 4; D_{y}|=|3|− 1; − 1|3|; = 3 ⋅ 3 − (− 1) ⋅ (− 1); = 8]

Content:
Finally, the solution to the system is given by
[MATH: x|= (D_{x})/(D) = (4)/(4) = 1,; y|= (D_{y})/(D) = (8)/(4) = 2.]

Content:
It is common to write the solutions to a linear system as a vector. So, in this case, we have
[MATH: \left< x,y \right> = \left< 1,2 \right>.]

---
